nameStory: The Beautiful Wood-nymph gets its enchanting name from its delicate appearance and woodland habitat, evoking mythical forest spirits from ancient folklore. The "beautiful" part of the name likely refers to its subtle but elegant wing patterns, though ironically this moth has evolved to look like something far less appealing - bird droppings!
description: The Beautiful Wood-nymph is a medium-sized moth in the cutworm moth family that has mastered the art of disguise. When resting during the day, it folds its wings to perfectly mimic a fresh bird dropping on a leaf or branch. This clever camouflage helps it avoid becoming a meal for hungry birds. Like other moths, it's most active at night when it comes to lights and feeds on flower nectar.

idTips.label: Bird dropping mimicry
idTips.description: At rest, appears as a convincing white and brown bird dropping with a glossy, wet-looking sheen that makes it look freshly deposited

idTips.label: Wing position
idTips.description: Folds wings tightly over its body in a distinctive triangular shape, completely hiding the colorful underwings

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized moth with wings spanning about 1.5-2 inches across, roughly the size of a half-dollar coin

idTips.label: Underwing colors
idTips.description: When wings open, reveals beautiful orange, yellow, and white patches that contrast dramatically with the drab outer appearance

idTips.label: Resting behavior
idTips.description: Sits motionless on leaves or bark during daylight hours, often on the upper surface of leaves where bird droppings would naturally land

habitat: Look for Beautiful Wood-nymphs in woodland edges, gardens, and areas with abundant grape vines, Virginia creeper, or buttonbush. They're particularly common around old stone walls and forest margins where their host plants climb and tangle. You'll often spot them resting on broad leaves of shrubs and small trees in partially shaded areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but are most easily found in early summer when they're actively mating and laying eggs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - adults are common at porch lights and flowers at night, while caterpillars feed on grape and Virginia creeper leaves.
seasonality.fall: Late-season adults may still be present in early fall, with caterpillars preparing to overwinter in leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as a pupa in the soil or leaf litter beneath host plants, completely hidden from view.

funFact: This moth is so committed to its bird dropping disguise that it even produces a special waxy coating on its wings that creates the glossy, wet appearance of fresh bird droppings - complete with realistic highlighting and shadows!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with actual bird droppings, which is exactly the point! The key difference is that real bird droppings don't have tiny antennae and won't suddenly unfold colorful wings when disturbed. Also distinguished from the Pearly Wood-nymph by having more brownish tones in its "dropping" disguise rather than pure white and black.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "wood-nymph," this moth is actually more commonly found around human habitation than deep in the woods, since many of its favorite host plants like grapes and Virginia creeper thrive in disturbed areas and garden settings.
compareHints: The Beautiful Wood-nymph differs from its close relative, the Pearly Wood-nymph, primarily in its bird dropping camouflage colors - the Beautiful has more brown and tan tones mixed with white, while the Pearly is more stark black and white. Both species use the same disguise strategy, but the Beautiful Wood-nymph's coloring tends to look like the droppings of fruit-eating birds, matching its preference for grape-growing areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Pearly Wood-nymph differs from its genus mate, the Beautiful Wood-nymph, primarily in wing coloration and sheen.
